title: Laredo trucking owner indicted in alleged scheme using 57 B-1 drivers on domestic routes
excerpt: A Laredo trucking company owner was indicted on federal charges alleging he recruited 57 drivers admitted under B-1 visas to haul domestic freight, saving the company nearly $300,000 in labor costs.
content:
A Laredo trucking company owner has been indicted on federal charges alleging he recruited drivers admitted to the United States under B-1 visas to haul freight between points inside the country, work their immigration status does not allow, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Texas.

Armando Martinez Varela, 56, of Laredo, owns VMS Transport LLC, a Laredo-based interstate trucking company. He faces charges of employment of unauthorized workers, encouraging or inducing unlawful entry or residence, harboring aliens, and making materially false statements to federal investigators, prosecutors said.

According to the indictment, Varela recruited drivers admitted under B-1 nonimmigrant status to transport domestic freight. B-1 status permits certain temporary business activities, including qualifying international transportation, but it does not authorize employment hauling freight solely within the United States, a practice known as cabotage.

Between Feb. 20 and May 15, 2026, company records allegedly showed 1,044 domestic transportation trips involving 57 B-1 visa drivers. The drivers allegedly picked up trailers in Laredo and delivered shipments throughout the United States, prosecutors said.

The indictment alleges VMS paid the B-1 drivers 25 to 50 cents per mile, compared with about 70 cents per mile for authorized drivers doing similar work. Federal authorities estimate the arrangement saved the company approximately $299,606 in labor costs. Prosecutors also allege Varela arranged housing for drivers between assignments rather than having them return to Mexico.

VMS Transport operates 53 power units and employs 50 drivers, according to federal motor carrier records, and its operating authority was listed as active as of Nov. 9.

If convicted, Varela faces up to 10 years in federal prison and a possible $250,000 fine. The investigation was conducted by Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Christine A. Cortez is prosecuting the case.

An indictment is a formal accusation of criminal conduct, not evidence of guilt. Varela is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

Sources: U.S. Department of Justice, Nov. 10, 2026; Laredo Morning Times, Nov. 11, 2026; FreightWaves, Nov. 11, 2026.
